content.text: Book reference: Chapter 10, pages 311–344. Guided Exercises: Accessing the Remote Command Line with SSH, Configuring SSH Key-Based Authentication, Customizing OpenSSH Service Configuration. Lab: Configuring and Securing SSH.
🎯 RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — This whole chapter

Generating and deploying SSH keys, then locking down sshd_config to require them (and to block root login) is one of the most frequently graded RHCSA tasks — practice the full key generation → copy → verify → harden sequence until it's automatic.

OpenSSH implements the SSH protocol — encrypted, authenticated remote command execution over an untrusted network. Beyond an interactive login, ssh can also run a single command remotely without opening a shell at all:
ssh remotehost # login as your current local username
ssh user02@remotehost # login as a specific user
ssh user02@remotehost hostname # run one command remotely, output shows up locally, no shell opened
w on the remote end shows exactly who's logged in and from where — useful for confirming a connection landed where you expected.
How host keys protect you from impersonation

Every SSH server has its own host key pair. The first time you connect to a given server, ssh has no record of its key and asks you to confirm the fingerprint before proceeding — accepting saves that key into your known_hosts file. Every later connection compares the server's current key against that saved copy automatically, with no prompt, as long as they match.
Location
Scope
~/.ssh/known_hosts
Per-user — keys this specific account has accepted
/etc/ssh/ssh_known_hosts
System-wide — administrator-populated, shared by everyone on the box
🎯 RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — A changed host key is a real security signal, not just an annoyance

If a saved key ever stops matching what the server presents, ssh refuses to connect automatically and warns loudly instead — that's exactly the scenario where traffic could be hijacked or the server has been rebuilt/compromised. Setting StrictHostKeyChecking yes (in ~/.ssh/config or system-wide /etc/ssh/ssh_config) makes ssh abort outright on any mismatch rather than merely asking. If a server's key changes for a KNOWN legitimate reason (disk replaced, OS reinstalled), the fix is editing known_hosts to remove the stale entry — never blindly accepting whatever the client suggests.
A server's own host key files live in /etc/ssh/, named like ssh_host_ecdsa_key.pub, ssh_host_rsa_key.pub, ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub — these are what get compared against your known_hosts entries.

Key-based auth uses a matched public/private key pair instead of a password. The private key stays secret on your machine (never copied anywhere); the public key is copied to every server you want to reach and used to verify you hold the matching private key — without the private key itself ever crossing the network.
ssh-keygen # defaults: ~/.ssh/id_rsa (private) and ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub (public)
ssh-keygen -f .ssh/key-with-pass # save to a custom, non-default path
File
Required permissions
Private key
600 (owner read/write only — ssh refuses to use an over-permissive private key file)
Public key
⚠ WARNING — Passphrase choice is a real security tradeoff, not a formality

An empty passphrase (just pressing Enter through the prompts) means anyone who obtains the private key file can use it immediately, with nothing else needed — convenient for automation, but that convenience IS the risk. A passphrase-protected key needs BOTH the file and the passphrase, so a stolen key alone isn't enough — but you'll be prompted for that passphrase on every single use unless you also run ssh-agent.
ssh-copy-id -i .ssh/key-with-pass.pub user@remotehost # installs your public key into that account's authorized_keys on the remote end
ssh -i .ssh/key-with-pass user@remotehost # log in using that specific private key
⚠ WARNING — Regenerating overwrites id_rsa/id_rsa.pub by default

Running ssh-keygen again without specifying a different file prompts to overwrite your existing default keypair. If you do overwrite it, every server that had your old public key installed needs the NEW public key re-copied with ssh-copy-id — the old servers won't accept the new key automatically.
ssh-agent — caching a passphrase for the session

A passphrase-protected key normally means retyping the passphrase every single time. ssh-agent caches it in memory for your session instead, so subsequent logins with that key are fully automatic — genuine passwordless convenience without giving up the safety of a passphrase-protected key.
eval $(ssh-agent) # starts the agent, sets env vars this shell needs to talk to it
ssh-add # add the default key, prompts once for its passphrase
ssh-add .ssh/key-with-pass # add a specific non-default key

eval $(...) matters here — ssh-agent on its own just PRINTS the shell commands needed to set its environment variables; eval actually executes them in your current shell so ssh-add and later ssh calls can find the running agent.
The daemon is sshd; its configuration file is /etc/ssh/sshd_config (note: NOT the same file as the client-side ssh_config mentioned above — client config vs. server config are two separate files).
Blocking direct root login
🎯 RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — Why this is a standard hardening step

root is a guaranteed username on every Linux box — an attacker only needs to guess the password, not the username too. root also has unlimited privileges, so a compromised root login is maximum-damage by definition. And forcing admins to log in as themselves, then escalate via su/sudo, creates an audit trail of WHO did what — direct root logins erase that accountability.
PermitRootLogin value
Effect
yes (the default)
Root can log in directly, by password or key
no
Root cannot log in over SSH at all, by any method
without-password
Root can log in via key-based auth only — password login as root is refused
# in /etc/ssh/sshd_config:
PermitRootLogin no
Requiring key-based authentication only
# in /etc/ssh/sshd_config:
PasswordAuthentication no
⚠ WARNING — Lock yourself out before you check this — a real, common mistake

If you disable PasswordAuthentication before confirming your key is ALREADY installed and working in that account's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, you can permanently lock yourself out of password-based access with no key to fall back on. Always verify key-based login succeeds FIRST, in a separate still-open session, before disabling passwords in this file.
Applying the change
sudo systemctl reload sshd
🎯 RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — reload, not restart — this is the same trap from Chapter 9, here with real consequences

reload re-reads sshd_config in place, with zero disruption to already-open SSH sessions — including the very session you're using to make the change. restart would work too, but it stops and restarts the whole daemon, which can drop your current connection mid-edit, on the machine you're editing. reload is the correct choice specifically because you're changing the config remotely, over the same service you're modifying.

sections.title: Hands-on: practice these on your own lab

content.text: 1. On workstation: ssh-keygen (accept all defaults, empty passphrase for now) — confirm ~/.ssh/id_rsa and id_rsa.pub exist with ls -l ~/.ssh (check the 600/644 permissions).
2. ssh-copy-id student@servera — enter the password once to install the key.
3. ssh student@servera — confirm it logs in with NO password prompt this time.
4. sudo vim /etc/ssh/sshd_config on servera: set PermitRootLogin no. sudo systemctl reload sshd.
5. From workstation (a SEPARATE terminal, keeping your key-based session open): ssh root@servera — confirm it's now refused.

6. Only after confirming your student key-based login still works: set PasswordAuthentication no on servera, reload sshd again, then open a brand-new terminal and confirm ssh student@servera still logs in via key while a deliberately-wrong scenario (e.g. a user with no key installed) is refused.
1. Q1 — ssh suddenly warns that a remote host's key has changed and refuses to connect automatically. What are the two possible explanations, and what's the safe next step?
2. Q2 — You want root to be able to log in over SSH using a key, but never using a password. Which PermitRootLogin value achieves exactly that?
3. Q3 — Why is systemctl reload sshd preferred over systemctl restart sshd when you're editing sshd_config over an existing SSH session?
NOTE — Answers

Q1 — Either the server was legitimately rebuilt/its key was regenerated for a valid reason, or the connection is being intercepted/the server compromised. The safe move is to verify out-of-band (ask the server's admin, check via console access) before removing the old entry from known_hosts and reconnecting — never just accept the new key on faith because the client offered to.
Q2 — PermitRootLogin without-password.

Q3 — reload re-reads the config file in place without interrupting already-open connections, including the very session used to make the edit; restart fully stops and restarts the daemon, which can drop that same session mid-change.
ssh logs into a remote system (interactively or to run one command); host keys, saved in known_hosts, let the client detect server impersonation on later connections.
ssh-keygen generates a private/public key pair (600/644 permissions); ssh-copy-id installs the public key on a remote account; ssh-agent + ssh-add cache a passphrase for a whole session.

PermitRootLogin (yes/no/without-password) and PasswordAuthentication (yes/no) in /etc/ssh/sshd_config are the two standard hardening settings — verify key-based login works BEFORE disabling password auth, to avoid locking yourself out.
systemctl reload sshd applies config changes without dropping existing connections; restart would work but risks breaking the very session you're using to make the change.
